intro: Open rate is the share of successfully delivered emails that got opened. Enter opens and delivered to get the rate — and see why that number can run higher than it looks.

sections.heading: How Open Rate is calculated
sections.body: Open Rate = Opens ÷ Delivered, shown as a percentage — [the same opens-over-delivered shape Campaign Monitor uses](https://www.campaignmonitor.com/resources/knowledge-base/how-to-calculate-email-open-rates/), where delivered means the message was successfully accepted rather than bounced, and opens counts each delivered message as opened at most once. Delivered, not sent, is the denominator: a bounced email was never in a position to be opened, so counting it would understate the rate for reasons that have nothing to do with the email itself. Delivered isn't a guarantee of inbox placement, either — a message can be delivered and still land in spam or a promotions tab.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 2,500 ÷ 10,000 = 25.00%. A quarter of the emails that were successfully delivered registered as opened — though as the next section covers, "opened" doesn't mean quite what it used to.

sections.heading: Why open rate can run higher than real engagement
sections.body: [Apple's Mail Privacy Protection can load a message's remote content in the background shortly after delivery](https://support.apple.com/guide/mail/protect-email-privacy-mlhlp1205/mac), regardless of whether the recipient actually reads the email, and hides from senders whether a genuine open ever happened. Since it launched in 2021, a large and growing share of inboxes run mail clients with a feature like this on, so a meaningful portion of recorded opens can reflect that automatic background loading rather than genuine attention — which inflates the number of recipients recorded as opened, without it needing to inflate the rate above 100%. This calculator counts each delivered message as opened at most once, so the rate stays capped at 100% by definition; a separate total-open-events count, which includes repeat opens, is not what this metric measures.

sections.heading: Open Rate vs. CTOR and CTR
sections.body: Open Rate, click-to-open rate, and email [CTR](/calculators/ctr) all divide by something different. Open Rate is opens over delivered — did the message register as opened at all. CTOR is clicks over opens — of the people who opened, how many then clicked. Email CTR is clicks over delivered — of everyone the message was delivered to, how many clicked, independent of whether an open was ever recorded. Mail Privacy Protection can inflate recorded opens, which inflates CTOR's denominator (opens) right along with it, while CTR's denominator (delivered) isn't affected at all — which is part of why clicks, not opens, are increasingly treated as the steadier engagement signal.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Treating an open rate near 100% as a tracking error. It can be a real signal that a large share of the list is on a mail client with privacy protection on, not proof the number is broken.

Confusing this deduplicated open rate with a raw open-events count. Some platforms separately report "total opens" (every open event, including repeats and background pre-fetches), which can exceed delivered — that's a different, additional metric, not what this rate measures.

Reading a rising open rate over time as improving engagement without checking whether privacy-protection adoption grew over the same period, which can inflate the metric independent of anything about the emails themselves.

Using open rate alone to judge subject line or send-time performance. Clicks reflect a deliberate action background pre-fetching doesn't touch, which is why they're a steadier signal than opens for that specific question.

faq.a: Open rate is the percentage of successfully delivered emails that were recorded as opened, calculated as opens divided by delivered emails. Delivered means the message was accepted rather than bounced — it's not a guarantee of inbox placement, and bounced messages are excluded from the denominator since they were never in a position to be opened at all. Open rate is one of the oldest email engagement metrics, but it's become a noisier signal in recent years: privacy features on major mail clients, most notably Apple Mail, can load a message's content automatically in the background shortly after delivery, before a recipient ever looks at it. It's still tracked and reported everywhere, but reading it as a precise measure of genuine attention requires knowing that limitation.

faq.q: How do you calculate Open Rate?
faq.a: Divide opens by delivered emails: Open Rate = Opens ÷ Delivered. A campaign that delivered 10,000 emails and recorded 2,500 opens has an open rate of 2,500 ÷ 10,000 = 25.00%. Delivered, not sent, is the correct denominator — bounced emails were never accepted in the first place, so including them in the total would understate the rate for reasons unrelated to how the campaign actually performed. Most email platforms calculate and report this automatically, so it rarely needs to be computed by hand, but the formula matters for understanding what the number does and doesn't capture, especially once privacy features that can auto-load content are factored in.

faq.q: Why can Open Rate look inflated, even near 100%?
faq.a: The most common cause is Apple's Mail Privacy Protection, which can load a message's remote content — including the tracking pixel used to register an open — in the background shortly after delivery, regardless of whether the recipient ever actually reads it. Since a large and growing share of inboxes run mail clients with a feature like this on, a meaningful portion of recorded opens can reflect that automatic background loading rather than genuine attention, which is why a rate near 100% isn't necessarily suspicious. This calculator counts each delivered message as opened at most once, so its open rate is capped at 100% by definition; a raw total-open-events count (which includes repeat opens and background loads) is a separate, additional metric that this rate doesn't compute.

faq.q: Is Open Rate the same as CTOR?
faq.a: No. Open rate divides opens by delivered emails — everyone the message was delivered to, whether they opened it or not. Click-to-open rate (CTOR) divides clicks by opens — only the people who registered as having opened the email, checking how many of them then clicked something inside it. Because Mail Privacy Protection can inflate the number of recorded opens, it can also inflate CTOR's denominator, which can make CTOR look artificially low even when actual click behavior hasn't changed. Email CTR — clicks divided by delivered — sidesteps that problem entirely, since its denominator doesn't depend on whether an open was recorded at all.

faq.q: What is a good Open Rate?
faq.a: There's no universal good open rate — it depends on list quality, industry, send frequency, and how much of the list uses mail clients with automatic open-tracking like Apple Mail, all of which shift the number for reasons unrelated to how good the email actually was. A well-maintained, engaged list can post a strong open rate that a purchased or stale list never will, regardless of subject line quality. Given how much Mail Privacy Protection alone can shift this number upward, the most reliable comparison is your own list's open rate over time, or against a segment with a similar mail-client mix, rather than an external benchmark that has no idea what your list looks like.

qaNotes:
STANDARD depth (Batch 05). Formula/example independently verified: 2500/10000=0.25=25.00%, matches calculator-catalog.json's exampleOutput exactly. Comparison-note (Open Rate vs CTOR vs CTR) written independently from ctr.json's own existing 'ctr-vs-ctor' comparison-note - no shared sentences. No universal 'good open rate' benchmark. External sources: Campaign Monitor's own open rate formula/denominator definition, and Apple's own official Mail support documentation on Mail Privacy Protection (support.apple.com/guide/mail/protect-email-privacy-mlhlp1205/mac). Related Calculators: ctr, cr, roas verified live - forms a real user-journey chain (opened -> clicked -> converted -> revenue), since catalog's own relatedCalculators list for this slug is almost entirely non-live CRM/email-specific slugs with no viable same-domain alternative. 5 FAQs, 100-150 words each, independently word-counted.

CORRECTION PASS (production audit, P0): the original content imported the catalog's own pre-existing validationRules/edgeCases text (which assumed TOTAL open-event semantics - 'opens > delivered can legitimately occur due to proxy pre-fetching, do not clamp to 100%') into content for what is, by name and convention, a standard unique-open-rate metric. This was a genuine numerator-semantics mismatch: standard email open-rate reporting (and this calculator's own name/single-output design) is a deduplicated unique-open concept, capped at 100% by definition, not a raw open-events count. Fixed: (1) removed all wording claiming a legitimate >100% open rate; (2) reframed the Apple Mail Privacy Protection section/FAQ around 'inflated recorded-opener counts approaching but not exceeding 100%,' explicitly naming total-open-events as a separate metric this calculator does not compute; (3) softened 'every Apple Mail user... registers as an open' to 'a meaningful portion of recorded opens can reflect automatic background loading' (non-absolute, since behavior varies by ESP/tracking implementation); (4) replaced 'delivered means emails that reached an inbox' with 'delivered means accepted rather than bounced, not a guarantee of inbox placement' throughout (formula section, both intro-adjacent FAQs). Runtime validation was also a real bug under this corrected definition: calc-validate.ts previously allowed opens > delivered with no error; added a scoped cross-field check (CROSS_FIELD_CHECKS['open-rate']) that now rejects opens > delivered as an input error, so the runtime can no longer accept a mathematically impossible state under the unique-open-rate definition this content now asserts.
